title: Containers (Advanced): Azure Kubernetes Service
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain how Kubernetes keeps a desired state with pods, deployments, services, probes and resource requests.
- Describe what Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) runs for you and what you still own: control plane, node pools, the node resource group, pricing tiers and AKS Automatic.
- Choose a network model, an IP plan and an ingress option for an AKS cluster.
- Plan scaling, identity, upgrades and monitoring, and decide between AKS and Azure Container Apps.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Six months after the storefront moved into containers, Dewi's team has split it into services: catalogue, cart, checkout, and a promotions engine that reprices hundreds of products every hour during a sale. A loyalty-points vendor ships its product as a Helm chart with its own Kubernetes operator, and Rizky insists that only a real Kubernetes cluster can run it.

Pak Budi has one condition: nothing in the cluster may clash with head office's 10.0.0.0/16 network, because a VPN to Azure is coming. Ibu Sari has two: "I am not hiring a team just to babysit servers," and "show me what it costs at three in the morning."

Today you find out what AKS runs for you, what stays your job, and how to set up a cluster that heals itself, scales with the 12.12 crowd and updates without downtime. You will also find out when not to use it.

Reading

1. Kubernetes in one lunch: desired state

Kubernetes is a container orchestrator. You do not tell it "start three containers on server 2"; you describe the desired state ("three copies of storefront v1 should always be running") in a YAML manifest, and Kubernetes works continuously to make reality match. Each controller runs a reconciliation loop: compare desired with actual, act on the difference, repeat. That loop is why Kubernetes heals itself.

A cluster has two halves. The control plane is the brain: the API server is the front door that every command goes through, etcd is the database that stores desired and actual state, the scheduler chooses a node for each new pod, and the controller manager runs the reconciliation loops. The nodes are the muscle: virtual machines that run a kubelet (the node agent), a container runtime (containerd) and kube-proxy, which programs service networking.

You will meet a handful of objects again and again:

Object | What it does | Nusantara Retail example
Pod | Smallest unit: one or more containers sharing an IP address and volumes | One copy of the storefront web server
Deployment | Keeps N identical pods running and rolls out new versions gradually | storefront, three replicas, image v1
Service | A stable name and virtual IP in front of changing pods | storefront, reachable inside the cluster as storefront.nusa
Namespace | A folder for objects, with its own permissions and quotas | nusa for the shop, loyalty for the vendor's chart
ConfigMap / Secret | Settings and sensitive values injected into pods | Promotion settings; a database connection string
Ingress / Gateway | Layer-7 entry: one address, routing by host name or path, TLS | shop.nusantara.example/cart to the cart service
HorizontalPodAutoscaler | Changes a deployment's replica count based on metrics | 3 to 10 storefront pods during the sale

Deployments are only one kind of workload. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable name and its own persistent disk, for software such as a message broker. A DaemonSet runs exactly one pod on every node, which suits log and security agents. A Job runs pods to completion, and a CronJob starts Jobs on a schedule, like the nightly price import from Lunch 13.

Two details in every good pod template decide how well the cluster can look after you. Probes tell Kubernetes about health. A readiness probe answers "may this pod receive traffic yet?", so a service sends requests only to ready pods. A liveness probe answers "is this process stuck?", and a failure restarts the container. A startup probe gives slow starters time before the other two begin. Resource requests and limits describe the pod's appetite. The scheduler places pods using their requests; a pod that exceeds its CPU limit is throttled, and one that exceeds its memory limit is killed (OOMKilled) and restarted.

spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: storefront
          image: mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v1
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi }    # what the scheduler reserves
            limits:   { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }  # the hard ceiling
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 } }   # gate for traffic
          livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 } }   # restart if stuck

Self-healing is real, but it is not instant. If a container crashes, the kubelet restarts it within seconds. If a whole node stops responding, Kubernetes marks it NotReady and, by default, evicts its pods after about five minutes; the Deployment controller then creates replacements on healthy nodes. That is why one replica is never enough for anything that matters, and why replicas should be spread across nodes and zones.

New versions roll out the same declarative way. Change the image tag in the manifest and apply it: the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods across gradually, as fast as maxSurge (extra pods allowed) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed to be missing) permit, and only as fast as new pods pass their readiness probes. If something goes wrong, kubectl rollout undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds.

2. AKS: what Azure runs, and what you run

Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) gives you a Kubernetes cluster whose control plane Microsoft runs, patches and keeps highly available. You never see those control-plane machines. On the Free tier there is no charge for cluster management; you pay for what runs in your subscription: the node VMs, their disks, load balancers, public IP addresses and outbound data.

Every cluster spans two resource groups. The one you choose holds only the cluster resource. AKS creates a second, the node resource group (named like MC_rg-lunch29-ab12c_aks-nusa_southeastasia), and fills it with the infrastructure: a Virtual Machine Scale Set per node pool, the virtual network, the load balancer, public IP addresses and managed disks. AKS owns that group. Changing things in it by hand is unsupported and can break the cluster, and AKS deletes it automatically when you delete the cluster.

Nodes are grouped into node pools, each a set of identical VMs. A system node pool hosts critical add-ons such as CoreDNS and metrics-server. It must run Linux, it cannot use B-series burstable sizes, and AKS blocks sizes smaller than about 2 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory. Production guidance asks for at least three nodes, and larger ones, because system pods need headroom. User node pools run your applications: Linux or Windows, any suitable size, and they can scale to zero. Adding the taint CriticalAddonsOnly=true:NoSchedule to the system pool keeps application pods off it. In regions with availability zones, a node pool can be spread across zones 1, 2 and 3, and the control plane is spread across zones automatically.

You talk to the cluster with kubectl. The command az aks get-credentials downloads a kubeconfig file that tells kubectl where the API server is and how to sign in; Cloud Shell already has kubectl installed. By default the API server has a public endpoint protected by authentication. For production you can restrict it to authorized IP ranges, or make the cluster private so that the API server is reachable only from your network. Scale and upgrade nodes through AKS (az aks scale, az aks nodepool, az aks upgrade), never through the scale set or VM APIs, and stop a whole dev cluster overnight with az aks stop.

Pricing tier | Use it for | What you get
Free | Learning, development, tests; recommended for fewer than 10 nodes | Free cluster management, all AKS features, no financially backed uptime SLA
Standard | Production | Uptime SLA for the API server (99.95% with availability zones, 99.9% without), more control-plane capacity, up to 5,000 nodes
Premium | Production that must stay on one Kubernetes version longer | Everything in Standard plus Long-Term Support: about two years per version instead of one

There are also two ways to run AKS. AKS Standard (the lab's choice, so that you see every part) lets you choose everything: node pools, VM sizes, network plugin, add-ons and upgrade settings. AKS Automatic, which Microsoft now recommends as the production default, makes those choices for you. It provisions nodes automatically to fit your pods, uses Azure CNI Overlay powered by Cilium, managed ingress, workload identity and Azure RBAC, upgrades itself, and runs on the Standard tier with an uptime SLA plus a pod-readiness SLA. Choose Automatic unless you need a setting it locks.

3. Networking: addresses, services and the way in

Pods need IP addresses, and the network model decides where those addresses come from.

Model | How pods get IP addresses | Use it when
Azure CNI Overlay | From a private pod range (CIDR) that is separate from the virtual network; each node gets a /24 slice, and traffic leaving the cluster uses the node's IP address | The default for new clusters and the recommended choice: scales to 5,000 nodes and up to 250 pods per node without using up virtual-network addresses
Azure CNI Pod Subnet | Real virtual-network addresses from a dedicated pod subnet | Resources outside the cluster must reach pods directly
Azure CNI Node Subnet | Virtual-network addresses from the node subnet | Legacy clusters only
kubenet | A private range with route tables | Retiring on 31 March 2028: migrate to Azure CNI Overlay

Azure CNI powered by Cilium is a data plane you can combine with Overlay: it uses eBPF instead of iptables and enforces network policies, the rules that decide which pods may talk to which. AKS Automatic uses it by default.

Plan three address ranges before you create a cluster, because they are hard or impossible to change later: the node subnet, the pod CIDR and the service CIDR, which gives every Kubernetes service its virtual IP address. None of them may overlap a network you will ever connect to. Here is Pak Budi's trap: the default service CIDR is 10.0.0.0/16, exactly head office's range. The lab sets --service-cidr 172.16.0.0/16 and --pod-cidr 192.168.0.0/16 to stay clear of it.

A service of type ClusterIP (the default) is reachable only inside the cluster, through a DNS name such as storefront.nusa.svc.cluster.local. Type LoadBalancer asks AKS to program the Azure Standard Load Balancer and attach a public IP address from the node resource group; an annotation makes it an internal load balancer instead.

Traffic leaving the cluster needs a plan too. By default nodes go out through the Standard Load Balancer's outbound rules. You can switch the outbound type to a managed NAT gateway or your own, or send everything through Azure Firewall with a user-defined route, which is how the hub-and-spoke design from Lunch 25 would inspect it. Inside the cluster, every pod can reach every other pod until you add network policies, such as "only checkout may call payments".

A load balancer works at layer 4, so you would need one public IP address per service. For HTTP routing by host name or path, with TLS, you add ingress. Kubernetes has two APIs for it: the older Ingress API, and the Gateway API, its role-oriented successor (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute). On AKS, the recommended managed option is the application routing add-on with its Gateway API implementation (gateway class approuting-istio). The alternatives are Application Gateway for Containers and the Istio service-mesh add-on.

Warning: Don't start new work on NGINX-based ingress. The upstream Ingress NGINX project is retired (its maintenance ended in March 2026), and Microsoft provides critical security patches for the application routing add-on's NGINX only until November 2026. Plan for the Gateway API.

4. Scaling and identity: both come in layers

Scaling in AKS happens at several layers, and each one solves a different problem:

Layer | What it scales | Triggered by
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) | The number of pods in a deployment | CPU or memory use as a percentage of requests, or custom metrics; by default it checks every 15 seconds and waits five minutes before scaling in
KEDA (add-on) | Pods, including down to zero | Events such as queue length, Kafka lag or a schedule
Vertical Pod Autoscaler (add-on) | Each pod's requests and limits | Observed usage, to right-size pods
Cluster autoscaler | Nodes in a node pool, within a minimum and maximum | Pods stuck in Pending because no node has room; empty, underused nodes are removed
Node autoprovisioning (NAP) | New nodes of whichever VM size fits | Pending pods; the default in AKS Automatic

They work as a chain. When the 12.12 crowd arrives, the HPA asks for more storefront pods. If the nodes have room, new pods start in seconds. If not, the extra pods wait in Pending, and the cluster autoscaler (or NAP) adds a node, which takes a few minutes. Everything depends on honest requests: without CPU requests the HPA cannot compute a percentage, and with inflated requests you pay for nodes that sit half empty.

The HPA's arithmetic is proportional. Three pods averaging 100% of their CPU request against a 50% target gives ceil(3 × 100 ÷ 50) = 6 pods, capped at the HPA's maximum. When the load drops, the count comes down again, but only after the five-minute stabilization window, so a short lull does not cause flapping.

Identity also comes in three layers, one for each direction of trust:

- People and pipelines into the cluster. Integrate the cluster with Microsoft Entra ID and authorize with Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes. AKS Standard starts with local accounts, which are fine for a lab; production clusters should disable them so that every kubectl command is tied to a real identity.
- The cluster into Azure. The cluster's managed identity creates load balancers and disks. A separate kubelet identity pulls images; az aks update --attach-acr gives it AcrPull on your registry, so no image pull secret is needed.
- Pods into Azure. Microsoft Entra Workload ID lets a pod exchange its Kubernetes service-account token for an Entra token through an OpenID Connect issuer and a federated credential. It replaces the older pod-managed identity preview, which is deprecated. Key Vault secrets reach pods through the Secrets Store CSI driver.

5. Day 2: upgrades, monitoring and cost

Kubernetes releases a minor version roughly every four months. AKS supports the newest generally available minor version and the two before it (N, N-1 and N-2), each for about twelve months; new clusters start on N-1. A version that falls to N-3 gets only platform support, and from June 2027 AKS upgrades clusters left on an unsupported version itself, after a 60-day grace period. In practice: plan to upgrade at least once a year, or choose the Premium tier with Long-Term Support if you truly cannot.

An upgrade goes control plane first, then node pools. For each node pool, AKS adds a surge node with the new version, cordons an old node (no new pods), drains it (evicts its pods so they reschedule elsewhere), and repeats. Your part is to make eviction safe: run at least two replicas, use readiness probes, and add a PodDisruptionBudget that says how many replicas must stay up. Node operating-system images get weekly security updates on a separate track. Auto-upgrade channels (for example patch or stable) and a node OS upgrade channel automate both, and planned maintenance windows keep them out of business hours.

Before a manual upgrade, az aks get-upgrades lists the versions you can move to, and AKS stops an upgrade when it detects workloads still calling Kubernetes APIs that the target version no longer serves. Keep kubectl within one minor version of the cluster.

For visibility, Container insights sends container logs and inventory to a Log Analytics workspace, the Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus collects metrics, and Azure Managed Grafana (or Azure Monitor dashboards with Grafana) draws them. Lunch 30 goes deeper. Day to day, kubectl get events, kubectl describe and kubectl top answer most "why is this pod unhappy?" questions.

Tip: The bill is mostly nodes, and nodes cost money whether they are busy or idle. Set realistic requests so pods pack tightly, enable the cluster autoscaler with sensible limits, run interruptible work on Spot user pools, use the Free tier for dev and test, stop dev clusters at night with az aks stop, and delete lab clusters as soon as you finish.

6. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail: AKS or Container Apps?

AKS is powerful because it gives you all of Kubernetes, and that is also its cost: someone must own upgrades, node pools, add-ons and YAML. Compare it honestly with Container Apps from Lunch 13:

Question | Azure Container Apps | Azure Kubernetes Service
Need the Kubernetes API (Helm charts with operators, CRDs, DaemonSets)? | Not available | Yes, the full API
Who handles nodes and upgrades? | The platform | You (much less with AKS Automatic)
Scale to zero | Built in for every app | Per workload with KEDA; nodes keep running unless a pool scales to zero
Pricing | Per second of use plus requests, with a free grant | Node VMs around the clock, plus the tier fee on Standard and Premium
Best fit | Web apps, APIs, workers and jobs from teams that just want to ship | Platform teams, complex microservices, vendor software built for Kubernetes

Your recommendation to Ibu Sari: the storefront stays on Container Apps, where it costs almost nothing at three in the morning. The microservices and the vendor's loyalty chart move to one AKS cluster, built as AKS Automatic in Indonesia Central once you have confirmed that the features you need are offered there. That gives Standard-tier SLAs, nodes across three zones, Azure CNI Overlay with Cilium, service and pod ranges that avoid 10.0.0.0/16, Gateway API ingress, Entra ID sign-in with Azure RBAC, Workload ID for Key Vault, images pulled from ACR by the kubelet identity, and Container insights with managed Prometheus from day one. One shared cluster, with a namespace and resource quota per team, costs far less than a cluster per application. And if the stores one day run small Kubernetes clusters of their own, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes can bring them under the same policies and monitoring (Lunch 31).

Pause and think: the three storefront replicas were all scheduled onto one node in zone 1. What happens to the shop if zone 1 fails, and which setting in the pod template would have prevented it? (Hint: look for topologySpreadConstraints in the lab's deployment.yaml.)

Next lunch, you will learn to ask the cluster's logs and metrics why checkout was slow on Friday.

Field notes from Stefanus

Drain a node on purpose before the cluster goes live. Before I sign off on any AKS cluster for production, I cordon and drain one node during working hours and watch the shop. It is the cheapest rehearsal of an upgrade I know. One drain exposes the single replica nobody noticed, the pod without a readiness probe that takes traffic too early, and the PodDisruptionBudget so strict that it blocks every drain, and with it every future upgrade. I also check where the replicas landed: three pods on one node are one pod as far as a failure is concerned. If the drain is boring, I trust the cluster. If it is exciting, I would much rather find out on a quiet Tuesday afternoon than in the middle of the 12.12 sale.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Overview of Azure CNI Overlay networking in AKS (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/concepts-network-azure-cni-overlay) — how pod addresses work, IP planning and how Overlay compares with kubenet.
- Microsoft Learn: AKS Free, Standard and Premium pricing tiers (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/free-standard-pricing-tiers) — what each tier includes and how to switch between them.
- Microsoft Learn: What is AKS Automatic? (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/intro-aks-automatic) — the preconfigured production defaults, compared feature by feature with AKS Standard.
- Microsoft Learn: Supported Kubernetes versions in AKS (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/aks/supported-kubernetes-versions) — the release calendar, the N-2 window, Long-Term Support and platform-initiated upgrades.

quiz.q: A new storefront pod shows Running, but the service never sends it any requests. Which probe is failing, and how does that differ from a failing liveness probe?
quiz.a: The readiness probe. A failing readiness probe keeps the pod out of the service's endpoints but leaves it running; a failing liveness probe makes the kubelet restart the container.

quiz.q: You create an HPA for the storefront, but kubectl get hpa shows the CPU target as <unknown>/50%, and nothing scales. What is the most likely cause?
quiz.a: The pods have no CPU requests (or metrics are not yet available). The HPA computes utilization as a percentage of requests, so without requests it has nothing to compare against.

quiz.q: Head office uses 10.0.0.0/16 and a VPN to Azure is planned. Which AKS address range is the hidden risk if you keep the defaults, and when must you fix it?
quiz.a: The service CIDR, which defaults to 10.0.0.0/16. Set a non-overlapping range such as 172.16.0.0/16 (and a non-overlapping pod CIDR) when you create the cluster, because these ranges are hard or impossible to change later.

quiz.q: Finance finds a resource group named MC_rg-lunch29-…_aks-nusa_southeastasia, full of VMs and a load balancer, and wants to delete it to save money. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: It is the node resource group that AKS owns. Don't change or delete resources in it by hand. Delete or scale the cluster instead; deleting the cluster deletes the node resource group automatically.

quiz.q: In October 2026, Rizky proposes the application routing add-on's managed NGINX for a brand-new ingress. What do you recommend instead?
quiz.a: The application routing add-on's Gateway API implementation (or Application Gateway for Containers, or the Istio add-on). Upstream Ingress NGINX is retired and Microsoft's patches for the add-on's NGINX end in November 2026.

takeaways: Kubernetes runs on desired state: you declare deployments, services, probes and requests, and controllers keep reality matching by restarting, rescheduling and rolling out pods.

AKS runs the control plane; you own the node pools, while the MC_ node resource group belongs to AKS. Use Free for dev and test, Standard for an SLA and Premium for Long-Term Support; AKS Automatic is the recommended production default.
Choose Azure CNI Overlay (kubenet retires in March 2028), plan node, pod and service ranges that never overlap your networks, and build ingress on the Gateway API, not on retiring NGINX.
Scaling and identity both come in layers: HPA, KEDA and the cluster autoscaler or NAP for capacity; Entra ID, managed identities and Workload ID for people, the cluster and pods.

Day 2 is the real work: upgrade within the N-2 window, protect upgrades with replicas, probes and PodDisruptionBudgets, monitor with Container insights and Prometheus, and pick Container Apps whenever you don't need the Kubernetes API.

lab.title: Kubernetes for the microservices team
lab.text:
What you'll build

Dewi's team needs a Kubernetes cluster for its microservices, and Ibu Sari needs proof that it heals itself, scales for the 12.12 sale and updates without closing the shop. You will create a small AKS cluster (Free tier, Azure CNI Overlay, one node) whose address ranges stay clear of head office's 10.0.0.0/16, and look inside both of its resource groups. Then you deploy the storefront from the manifests in k8s/: three replicas with probes and resource requests behind a public LoadBalancer service. You will delete pods and watch them return, roll out v2 without a single failed request, add a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and load it until new pods appear, and diagnose a broken image tag.

The app is a small Microsoft sample web server that listens on port 80 and shows the TITLE environment variable as its page title, so you can see at a glance which version answered.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)), with at least 2 free vCPUs of regional quota (4 if you want the stretch goals).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. kubectl is already installed there.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/29-containers-advanced-aks
source ../common/config.sh
RG=$(rg_name 29)
AKS=aks-nusa
AKS_NODE_SIZE=${AKS_NODE_SIZE:-Standard_D2s_v5}

- Check that the node size is offered to you and that you have quota. The size needs 2 vCPUs; free and trial subscriptions often have only 4 vCPUs in total per region:

az vm list-skus --location "$LOCATION" --size "$AKS_NODE_SIZE" --resource-type virtualMachines \
  --query "[].{size:name, zones:join(',', locationInfo[0].zones || \`[]\`), restricted:length(restrictions)}" --output table

az vm list-usage --location "$LOCATION" \
  --query "[?contains(localName, 'Total Regional') || contains(localName, 'DSv5')].{quota:localName, used:currentValue, limit:limit}" \
  --output table

az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerService --wait

If restricted is not 0, or the DSv5 family has no free quota, pick another non-burstable size with 2 vCPUs, for example AKS_NODE_SIZE=Standard_D2as_v5 or Standard_D2s_v4, and check again. B-series sizes are not allowed for a system node pool.

Important: This is a lab: the node VM, its disk, the load balancer and the public IP addresses cost money every hour the cluster exists. Do the lab in one sitting and run Clean up as soon as you finish, even if you stop halfway. If Cloud Shell times out, reopen it, cd back into this folder and re-run the source and variable lines above (plus IP= and NODE_RG= from the tasks).

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–5 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create a small AKS cluster

The cluster takes 5 to 10 minutes to create. Start it now and read the flag table while you wait.

ensure_rg "$RG" 29

az aks create \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$AKS" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --tier free \
  --node-count 1 \
  --node-vm-size "$AKS_NODE_SIZE" \
  --zones 1 2 3 \
  --network-plugin azure \
  --network-plugin-mode overlay \
  --pod-cidr 192.168.0.0/16 \
  --service-cidr 172.16.0.0/16 \
  --dns-service-ip 172.16.0.10 \
  --generate-ssh-keys \
  --output none

Flag | Why
--tier free | No charge for cluster management and no uptime SLA: right for a lab. Production uses Standard or Premium.
--node-count 1 --node-vm-size … | One system-pool node with 2 vCPUs, the smallest practical size. Production system pools have at least three nodes.
--zones 1 2 3 | The node pool may place nodes in all three zones. With one node you only use one, but the stretch goals add a second.
--network-plugin azure --network-plugin-mode overlay | Azure CNI Overlay: pods get addresses from a private pod range, not from your virtual network. If you set --network-plugin azure without the mode, AKS uses the older node-subnet mode, so state it explicitly.
--pod-cidr 192.168.0.0/16 | The pod range. It must not overlap any network the cluster will ever talk to.
--service-cidr 172.16.0.0/16 --dns-service-ip 172.16.0.10 | The default service range is 10.0.0.0/16, exactly Pak Budi's head-office network, so we move it.
--generate-ssh-keys | Uses your SSH key in ~/.ssh, or creates one if you have none.

While you wait, open the files in k8s/ (in Cloud Shell: code k8s/deployment.yaml) and find the replica count, the rolling-update settings, the probes, and the resource requests and limits.

When the command returns, look at what you created and connect kubectl:

az aks show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" \
  --query "{state:provisioningState, version:currentKubernetesVersion, tier:sku.tier, plugin:networkProfile.networkPlugin, mode:networkProfile.networkPluginMode, podCidr:networkProfile.podCidr, serviceCidr:networkProfile.serviceCidr}" \
  --output table

NODE_RG=$(az aks show --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --query nodeResourceGroup --output tsv)
echo "Node resource group: $NODE_RG"
az resource list --resource-group "$NODE_RG" --query "[].{name:name, type:type}" --output table

az aks get-credentials --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --overwrite-existing
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
kubectl get pods --namespace kube-system

Your resource group holds only the cluster resource. The node resource group, created and owned by AKS, holds the real infrastructure: a virtual machine scale set for the node pool, a virtual network, a network security group, a load balancer with an outbound public IP and a managed identity. Look, but don't change anything in it.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Kubernetes services › aks-nusa shows the same settings on Overview and Settings › Networking, and Kubernetes resources › Workloads lists the system pods without any kubectl. The Properties page links to the infrastructure (node) resource group.

Checkpoint: the state is Succeeded, the tier Free, the plugin azure in overlay mode, the service range 172.16.0.0/16, and kubectl get nodes shows one node with status Ready and a zone label.

Task 2 · Deploy the storefront from manifests

Manifests describe the desired state; kubectl apply hands it to the API server, and the controllers make it happen.

kubectl apply -f k8s/namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml -f k8s/service.yaml -f k8s/pdb.yaml
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
kubectl get deployment,pods,service,pdb --namespace nusa -o wide

The service asks Azure for a public IP address, which takes a minute or two. Watch it, and press Ctrl+C when EXTERNAL-IP shows an address instead of <pending>:

kubectl get service storefront --namespace nusa --watch

IP=$(kubectl get service storefront --namespace nusa -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')
echo "http://${IP}"
curl -s "http://${IP}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"

# The same service, seen from the Azure side:
az network public-ip list --resource-group "$NODE_RG" --query "[].{name:name, ip:ipAddress}" --output table

The PodDisruptionBudget from pdb.yaml promises that voluntary disruptions, such as a node drain during an upgrade, never take the storefront below two ready pods.

Checkpoint: READY shows 3/3, the service has an external IP address, curl prints <title>Nusantara Retail storefront v1</title>, and the same address appears in the node resource group.

Task 3 · Watch Kubernetes heal itself, then scale by hand

Delete a pod as if it had crashed, and watch the Deployment controller replace it:

kubectl get pods --namespace nusa
POD=$(kubectl get pods --namespace nusa -l app=storefront -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl delete pod "$POD" --namespace nusa --wait=false
kubectl get pods --namespace nusa --watch        # Ctrl+C after a few seconds
kubectl get events --namespace nusa --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 8

Now scale by hand, imperatively:

kubectl scale deployment storefront --namespace nusa --replicas=5
kubectl get pods --namespace nusa -o wide
kubectl scale deployment storefront --namespace nusa --replicas=3

kubectl scale changes the live object, not your file. The next kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml sets the count back to 3, so a declarative change in the file (or an autoscaler, in Task 5) is the lasting way to change it.

Checkpoint: the deleted pod is replaced by one with a new name within seconds, the events show Killing and Scheduled/Created/Started, and the deployment went to 5 replicas and back to 3.

Task 4 · Roll out v2 without dropping a request, then roll back

Start a background "shopper" that calls the site every half second for about 90 seconds and counts the HTTP status codes, then change the pod template:

( for i in $(seq 1 180); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --max-time 5 "http://${IP}/"; sleep 0.5; done | sort | uniq -c ) &
WATCH_PID=$!

kubectl set env deployment/storefront --namespace nusa TITLE="Nusantara Retail storefront v2"
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
wait "$WATCH_PID"

curl -s "http://${IP}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"
kubectl rollout history deployment/storefront --namespace nusa

The shopper's tally should show only 200. With maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, Kubernetes starts one new pod, waits for its readiness probe, removes one old pod, and repeats; the number of ready pods never drops below three.

Now pretend v2 has a bug and roll back to the previous ReplicaSet:

kubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
curl -s "http://${IP}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"

Checkpoint: the tally shows only 200 responses, the title changed to v2 and, after the undo, back to v1, and kubectl rollout history lists the revisions.

Task 5 · Autoscale pods with the HPA

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler measures CPU as a percentage of each pod's request (50m here). AKS includes metrics-server, so you can see the numbers it uses:

kubectl top pods --namespace nusa
kubectl apply -f k8s/hpa.yaml
kubectl get hpa storefront --namespace nusa

kubectl autoscale deployment storefront --namespace nusa --min=3 --max=10 --cpu=50% creates the same object imperatively (older kubectl versions use --cpu-percent=50). The YAML version works with every version and lives in source control.

Now generate load from inside the cluster with the provided pod (it runs for five minutes), and watch the HPA:

kubectl apply -f k8s/load-generator.yaml

for i in $(seq 1 16); do
  sleep 15
  kubectl get hpa storefront --namespace nusa --no-headers
done
kubectl get pods --namespace nusa -o wide

TARGETS climbs well above 50%, and REPLICAS rises towards 10. If some new pods stay Pending, the single node is full: that is exactly the moment a cluster autoscaler would add a node (stretch goal 3). When the load generator finishes, the HPA waits for its five-minute stabilization window and then scales back to 3. Remove the finished pod:

kubectl delete pod load-generator --namespace nusa --ignore-not-found

No luck with the load generator? Use Cloud Shell instead

end=$((SECONDS + 180))
while (( SECONDS < end )); do
  seq 1 300 | xargs -P 50 -I{} curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 5 "http://${IP}/"
done &
for i in $(seq 1 12); do sleep 15; kubectl get hpa storefront --namespace nusa --no-headers; done
wait

Tip: Prefer the portal? aks-nusa › Kubernetes resources › Workloads shows the pod count changing, and Monitoring › Metrics can chart node CPU while the load runs.

Checkpoint: during the load kubectl get hpa shows a CPU value above 50% and more than 3 replicas; a few minutes after the load stops, it is back to 3.

Break it and fix it

A colleague "upgrades" the storefront to a tag that does not exist:

kubectl set image deployment/storefront --namespace nusa storefront=mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v99
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront --namespace nusa --timeout=60s
kubectl get pods --namespace nusa
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://${IP}/"

Symptom: the rollout never finishes, and one new pod shows ErrImagePull and then ImagePullBackOff. Yet curl still returns 200. Find out why the pod is stuck, why the shop stayed open, and fix it.

Hint

Run kubectl describe pod <the-stuck-pod> --namespace nusa and read the Events at the bottom: the kubelet reports that it failed to pull mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v99 because the tag was not found. The shop stayed open because maxUnavailable: 0 keeps every old pod running until a new pod is ready, and this one never becomes ready.

Fix

kubectl rollout undo deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
# or: kubectl set image deployment/storefront --namespace nusa storefront=mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v1
kubectl rollout status deployment/storefront --namespace nusa
kubectl get pods --namespace nusa

The same message appears when a tag was deleted, a registry is private and the cluster has no pull permission (az aks update --attach-acr fixes that for ACR), or a node cannot reach the registry.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch29-<suffix>. Deleting the cluster inside it makes AKS delete the node resource group MC_rg-lunch29-<suffix>_aks-nusa_<region> as well, with the node VM, its disk, the load balancer and the public IP addresses, so you don't delete that group yourself. The script also removes the cluster from your kubeconfig. Deletion runs in the background and takes several minutes; run bash cleanup.sh again after about ten minutes to confirm that nothing is left (it also removes a node resource group left behind by a failed deployment).

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Operation could not be completed as it results in exceeding approved ... Cores quota | Not enough regional or VM-family vCPU quota | Delete other VMs or clusters, choose a size from a family with free quota (AKS_NODE_SIZE=...), or request more quota (not possible on Free Trial or Azure for Students)
The create fails because the VM size is not available, not allowed in your subscription, or not offered in a zone | The size is restricted for your subscription or region | Pick another 2-vCPU, non-B-series size, or remove the --zones 1 2 3 line
The create rejects the node size for a system node pool | AKS documentation is inconsistent about the minimum (one page says 2 vCPUs, another 4) | Use a 4-vCPU size such as Standard_D4s_v5 if your quota allows; it uses all 4 vCPUs of a trial quota
ManagedClusterCountExceedsQuotaLimit | Too many AKS clusters in this region for your subscription | Delete unused clusters (az aks list --output table)
MissingSubscriptionRegistration for Microsoft.ContainerService | Resource provider not registered | az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerService --wait
kubectl: Unable to connect to the server or You must be logged in to the server | Old or missing kubeconfig entry, or a new Cloud Shell session | az aks get-credentials --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --overwrite-existing, then kubectl config current-context
EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> for more than a few minutes | Azure is still creating the public IP, or a quota or policy blocks it | kubectl describe service storefront --namespace nusa and read the events
HPA TARGETS shows <unknown>/50% | Metrics are not available yet, or the pods have no CPU requests | Wait a minute after the pods start; make sure deployment.yaml still has resources.requests.cpu
New pods stay Pending with Insufficient cpu | The single node is full | Expected at the top of the load; lower maxReplicas, or add a node (stretch goals 2 and 3)
load-generator ends in Error or never starts | The busybox image could not be pulled or lacks a tool | Use the Cloud Shell alternative in Task 5
A pod shows ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff | Wrong image name or tag, or no permission to pull | See Break it and fix it

Stretch goals

Stretch goals 1–3 need a second node: 4 vCPUs in total. Check your quota first and scale back afterwards.

1. Ingress with the Gateway API. Enable the application routing add-on's Gateway API implementation (Azure CLI 2.86 or later), give it room, then apply k8s/gateway.yaml:
  az aks scale --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --node-count 2
  az aks update --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --enable-gateway-api --enable-app-routing-istio
  kubectl get pods --namespace aks-istio-system
  kubectl apply -f k8s/gateway.yaml
  kubectl wait --for=condition=programmed gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io/storefront-gateway --namespace nusa --timeout=300s
  GW=$(kubectl get gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io storefront-gateway --namespace nusa -o jsonpath='{.status.addresses[0].value}')
  curl -s "http://${GW}/" | grep -o "<title>[^<]*</title>"

  Don't build new ingress on the add-on's NGINX flavour: its Microsoft support ends in November 2026.
2. Zones and a node failure. With two nodes, check kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone and kubectl get pods --namespace nusa -o wide: the topology spread constraints place replicas on both nodes. Simulate maintenance with kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data, watch the pods move while the PodDisruptionBudget keeps two of them up, then kubectl uncordon <node-name>.
3. Cluster autoscaler. Let AKS add the second node only when pods are Pending:
  az aks update --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --enable-cluster-autoscaler --min-count 1 --max-count 2
  kubectl patch hpa storefront --namespace nusa --patch '{"spec":{"maxReplicas":20}}'

  Run the load again and watch kubectl get nodes --watch: a new node joins after a few minutes.
4. Container insights. Send container logs to a workspace inside the lab's resource group, so that clean-up removes it too:
  az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name log-nusa --output none
  WS_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show --resource-group "$RG" --workspace-name log-nusa --query id --output tsv)
  az aks enable-addons --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" --addons monitoring --workspace-resource-id "$WS_ID"

  After about ten minutes, open aks-nusa › Monitoring › Insights. Lunch 30 teaches you to query these logs with KQL.
5. Pause instead of delete (for longer projects). az aks stop --resource-group "$RG" --name "$AKS" stops the nodes and the control plane while keeping the configuration, and az aks start brings it all back. For this lab, deleting the cluster is still the cheapest option, and this guide recreates it in ten minutes.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (CLI, portal, Bicep, Terraform):

1. A resource group rg-lunch29-<suffix> in your lab region, created with ensure_rg "$(rg_name 29)" 29 so that cleanup.sh can find it.
2. An AKS cluster aks-nusa on the Free tier, using Azure CNI Overlay, with a system node pool of a non-B-series size, and with pod and service address ranges that do not overlap head office's 10.0.0.0/16.
3. In namespace nusa, a deployment storefront running mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aks-helloworld:v1 with at least 3 ready replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits, and readiness and liveness probes.
4. A service storefront of type LoadBalancer with a public IP address that answers HTTP 200.
5. A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler storefront for that deployment with a minimum of 3 and a maximum of 10 replicas and a CPU utilization target.
6. No pod in the namespace stuck in ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff.

Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode. Then delete the cluster.
